questions.question: For a 4-hour battery at ERCOT's hub average with perfect foresight, what was the total revenue over the last twelve complete months (2025-10 to 2026-09), in USD per kW?
questions.answer: The warehouse holds this figure in USD per MW, not USD per kW. For a 4-hour battery at ERCOT HB_HUBAVG with perfect foresight, total revenue (energy plus ancillary services) summed over the 12 months 2025-10 to 2026-09 is 81,402.19 USD/MW (battery_stack_monthly, derived). The variable is foresight_4h_revenue_total_usd_per_mw. Foresight is an upper bound: real-time energy and day-ahead ancillary services. No days were left out, and 365 days were held (battery_stack_monthly). I have not converted this to USD per kW, because I can't compute new numbers. The monthly values run from 3,596.91 USD/MW in 2026-06 to 14,626.59 USD/MW in 2026-01 (battery_stack_monthly). Months are local (Central time) months. The table includes no capacity payment, and the battery is a price taker, so these figures are idealised.

# ERCOT: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) runs the power grid for most of Texas. It is a grid operator, not a utility: it owns no power plants and no power lines. It schedules the plants that others own, keeps supply equal to demand every second, and runs the wholesale market where power is bought and sold. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Texas Legislature oversee it. Parts of Texas, near El Paso, in the Panhandle and in the east, belong to other grids.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

ERCOT runs two markets. In the day-ahead market, buyers and sellers agree today on power for each hour of tomorrow. In the real-time market, ERCOT dispatches plants every few minutes and pays the price at that moment. Prices are set at each location on the grid (locational marginal prices), so power costs more where lines are congested. A hub, such as the Hub Average on this page, averages many locations into one price that traders use. ERCOT has no capacity market: generators are paid only for the energy they sell and some reliability services, so prices during scarce hours can rise very high, which is meant to reward being available.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/mktinfo ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

ERCOT is an island. Its grid has only a few small links to the rest of the country and to Mexico, so it cannot lean on its neighbors in an emergency, and because its power does not cross state lines in a big way, the federal regulator (FERC) does not set its market rules. It is also the energy-only market described above. Texas produces more wind electricity than any other state (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/wind/where-wind-power-is-harnessed.php) and is adding large amounts of solar and batteries, so the mix on this page changes a lot between a windy night and a sunny afternoon.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/ERCO

## A short history

- **1970:** ERCOT is formed to manage reliability for the Texas grid (ERCOT, https://www.ercot.com/news/mediakit/backgrounder).
- **2010-12-01:** ERCOT starts its nodal market, with a price at each location on the grid instead of a few zones (ERCOT, https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2011/04/26/ercot_2010_financial_statements.pdf).
- **2021-02-15:** During Winter Storm Uri, ERCOT orders utilities to cut power to customers across the state because too many power plants had failed in the cold (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=46836).

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports ERCOT as balancing authority ERCO.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price.
- **Peak and off-peak:** peak hours are weekday daytime hours when demand is high; the rest are off-peak.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.
- **Interconnection queue:** the waiting list of new power plants and batteries asking to connect to the grid.

out.text:
# ERCOT: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) runs the power grid for most of Texas. It is a grid operator, not a utility: it owns no power plants and no power lines. It schedules the plants that others own, keeps supply equal to demand every second, and runs the wholesale market where power is bought and sold. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Texas Legislature oversee it. Parts of Texas, near El Paso, in the Panhandle and in the east, belong to other grids.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

ERCOT runs two markets. In the day-ahead market, buyers and sellers agree today on power for each hour of tomorrow. In the real-time market, ERCOT dispatches plants every few minutes and pays the price at that moment. Prices are set at each location on the grid (locational marginal prices), so power costs more where lines are congested. A hub, such as the Hub Average on this page, averages many locations into one price that traders use. ERCOT has no capacity market: generators are paid only for the energy they sell and some reliability services, so prices during scarce hours can rise very high, which is meant to reward being available.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/mktinfo ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

ERCOT is an island. Its grid has only a few small links to the rest of the country and to Mexico, so it cannot lean on its neighbors in an emergency, and because its power does not cross state lines in a big way, the federal regulator (FERC) does not set its market rules. It is also the energy-only market described above. Texas produces more wind electricity than any other state (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/wind/where-wind-power-is-harnessed.php) and is adding large amounts of solar and batteries, so the mix on this page changes a lot between a windy night and a sunny afternoon.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/ERCO

## A short history

- **1970:** ERCOT is formed to manage reliability for the Texas grid (ERCOT, https://www.ercot.com/news/mediakit/backgrounder).
- **2010-12-01:** ERCOT starts its nodal market, with a price at each location on the grid instead of a few zones (ERCOT, https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2011/04/26/ercot_2010_financial_statements.pdf).
- **2021-02-15:** During Winter Storm Uri, ERCOT orders utilities to cut power to customers across the state because too many power plants had failed in the cold (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=46836).

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports ERCOT as balancing authority ERCO.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price.
- **Peak and off-peak:** peak hours are weekday daytime hours when demand is high; the rest are off-peak.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.
- **Interconnection queue:** the waiting list of new power plants and batteries asking to connect to the grid.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us.php

# CAISO: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) runs the high-voltage grid for most of California and a small part of Nevada. It is a nonprofit grid operator: it owns no power plants, schedules the plants that others own, keeps supply equal to demand, and runs the wholesale market. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules, and California's energy agencies set the state's energy policy. Some California utilities, such as the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District, run their own balancing areas outside CAISO.

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/about ; https://www.caiso.com/about/our-business ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

CAISO runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes at the price of that moment. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices). Trading hubs summarize them: NP15 in the north, ZP26 in the middle and SP15 in the south; this page uses SP15. CAISO also runs a real-time market for utilities across the West, which lets them trade power with California every few minutes.

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/about/our-business ; https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

Sunshine. California produces more solar electricity than any other state (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/solar/where-solar-is-found.php), so in the middle of a sunny day the grid can have more power than it needs: prices fall, sometimes below zero, and some solar is turned off (curtailed). When the sun sets, solar output drops just as people come home, and other plants and batteries must ramp up quickly. This evening ramp is why California has built so many batteries, which charge at midday and discharge in the evening: you can see that daily cycle in the battery block on this page.

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/todays-outlook ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/CISO

## A short history

- **1998-03-31:** CAISO begins operating the grid, after California restructured its electricity industry (CAISO, https://www.caiso.com/documents/rtofiling.pdf).
- **2014-11-01:** The Western Energy Imbalance Market starts, letting utilities outside California trade power with CAISO in real time (CAISO, https://www.caiso.com/content/monthly-market-performance/dec-2022/western-energy-imbalance-market.html).
- **2020-08-14:** During a West-wide heat wave, CAISO orders rotating outages because demand outran the power available (CAISO, https://www.caiso.com/Documents/Final-Root-Cause-Analysis-Mid-August-2020-Extreme-Heat-Wave.pdf).

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/about ; https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports CAISO as balancing authority CISO.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price. SP15 is Southern California's.
- **Curtailment:** turning down solar or wind that could have produced, because the grid cannot use or move the power.
- **Evening ramp:** the fast rise in other generation needed as solar output falls at sunset.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.caiso.com/todays-outlook

# SPP: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Southwest Power Pool (SPP) runs the power grid and wholesale market across the central Great Plains, from the Dakotas and Montana south through Nebraska, Kansas and Oklahoma to parts of Texas, New Mexico, Arkansas and Louisiana (SPP, https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/). It owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that its members own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/ ; https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/ ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

SPP's market, the Integrated Marketplace, has a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices) and summarized at trading hubs; this page uses the SPP North Hub. SPP has no capacity auction: its members must show they have enough capacity themselves.

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

Wind. The Great Plains are among the windiest places in the country, and on windy nights wind can supply a large share of SPP's power (SPP, https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/), pushing some prices to zero or below. Because the wind is strongest far from cities, getting it to customers depends on long transmission lines, and SPP curtails wind when the lines are full: the curtailment tracker on this site shows it.

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/SWPP

## A short history

- **1941:** Utilities in the region pool their power to keep an aluminum plant in Arkansas running for the war effort; SPP grows from this pool (SPP, https://www.spp.org/news-list/spp-celebrates-20-years-as-an-rto-with-growth-and-added-value-for-members/).
- **2014:** SPP launches the Integrated Marketplace, with day-ahead and real-time markets (SPP, https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/).
- **2021-02-15:** During Winter Storm Uri, SPP directs utilities to cut power to some customers to protect the grid (SPP, https://spp.org/documents/65037/comprehensive%20review%20of%20spp's%20response%20to%20the%20feb.%202021%20winter%20storm%202021%2007%2019.pdf).

Sources: https://www.spp.org/about-us/ ; https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports SPP as balancing authority SWPP.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Integrated Marketplace:** SPP's day-ahead and real-time markets.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price; this page uses the SPP North Hub.
- **Curtailment:** turning down wind or solar that could have produced, because the grid cannot use or move the power.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.spp.org/about-us/fast-facts/

Tables with in_live_set no cannot be queried here (their full history is on Redivis). first, last and rows describe the whole ERW table, not the live set. Internal tables are not visible here.
